1.title: Liquids and Gases Flow
1.text:
Liquids and Gases Flow

Fluids are materials that can flow and have no definite shape of their own.

Our big question for this lesson: what is a fluid, and what are its properties? Let's head out onto a frozen lake.

The chunks of ice in Figure 1 have a set mass and a set shape, no matter how big the lake is. When the ice melts, the mass stays the same, but the shape changes. The water flows to fill the lake basin and forms a flat top surface. As some of it evaporates, it becomes water vapor, which also flows and has no shape of its own.

Liquids and gases are both fluids: materials that can flow and have no definite shape of their own. In both, the atoms and molecules have lots of freedom to move. And the fluid filling the space above the water in Figure 1? That's air, another fluid!

testIt.name: Melting ice
testIt.how: Tap to melt a 1.0 L block of ice into a different container. The water takes its shape; the volume stays put.

In Review the News, you'll find a current news story about the properties or behavior of fluids, evaluate the source, and share what you learn with your class.

3.title: What Is Pressure?
3.text:
What Is Pressure?

Pressure is the perpendicular component of a force on a surface divided by the area of the surface: P equals F over A.

You've probably heard of water pressure and air pressure. Pressure and force are related, but they're not the same thing. Pressure is the perpendicular part of a force on a surface divided by the area of that surface: P equals F over A. Because pressure comes from a force, anything that exerts pressure can cause change and do work. In Figure 2, both the astronaut and the landing module's legs press on the Moon's surface.

Let's try one! The lunar module weighed about 12,000 newtons and rested on four pads, each 91 centimeters across. Each pad's area is pi times the square of 0.455 meters, about 0.65 square meters, so the four pads total about 2.6 square meters. That gives a pressure of about 4.6 kilopascals. To estimate the astronaut's pressure, you'd divide the astronaut's weight on the Moon by the area of the boot soles.

Pressure is a scalar. Its SI unit is the pascal, one newton per square meter. A pascal is tiny, about the pressure of a flat dollar bill on a table, so we usually use kilopascals, where 1 kilopascal is 1000 pascals. Standard atmospheric pressure, from Table 1, is 101.325 kilopascals.

4.title: Pressure in Solids, Liquids, and Gases
4.text:
Pressure in Solids, Liquids, and Gases

In the kinetic-molecular model, gas pressure comes from the impulses of particles colliding with a container's surface.

Picture yourself standing on a frozen lake. Your weight is spread over your shoe soles, so you put pressure on the ice. The forces holding the vibrating water molecules in place let the ice push up on your feet with a force equal to your weight. If the ice melted, most of those bonds would weaken. The molecules would stay close but slide past one another, and you'd fall through, though the moving molecules would still push on you.

For gases, we use the kinetic-molecular theory, which describes an ideal gas: particles that take up no space and don't attract each other. Real gas particles do take up space and attract a little, but the ideal gas is an accurate model under most conditions. In this model, gas particles zoom around randomly at high speed and collide elastically. When one hits a wall, it bounces back, changing its momentum. The impulses from all these collisions are the gas pressure.

A material's molecular structure at a given temperature and pressure lets you predict its state and some of its properties. Fluids flow because their particles are free to move past each other.

5.title: Atmospheric Pressure
5.text:
Atmospheric Pressure

At sea level, the atmosphere exerts about 10 newtons on each square centimeter, about 100 kilopascals.

At sea level, the air pushes in all directions with about 10 newtons on every square centimeter, about the weight of a 1-kilogram object. Your body pushes outward so evenly that you hardly notice. You probably only feel it when your ears pop in a fast elevator or an airplane.

Since a square centimeter is 10 to the negative fourth square meters, that's about 1.0 times 10 to the fifth newtons per square meter, or 100 kilopascals. Other planets have atmospheres too. On the surface of Venus, the pressure is about 92 times what it is on Earth!

testIt.name: Elevator
testIt.how: Ride the elevator up and watch the air pressure drop (about 1.2 kPa per 100 m near the ground).

6.title: Example Problem 1, A Child on a Stool
6.text:
Example Problem 1, A Child on a Stool

The same force over a smaller area makes a greater pressure.

A child weighing 364 newtons sits on a three-legged stool weighing 41 newtons. The legs touch the ground over a total of 19.3 square centimeters. What's the average pressure on the ground? And what happens when the child leans so only two legs touch?

Step one: analyze and sketch. Sketch the child and stool with the total force on the ground. Known: the child's weight is 364 newtons and the stool's weight is 41 newtons, so the total is 405 newtons. Area a is 19.3 square centimeters. Area b is two-thirds of that, 12.9 square centimeters. Unknown: pressures a and b.

Step two: solve with P equals F over A. For part a, divide 405 newtons by 19.3 square centimeters, and convert using 100 centimeters per meter, squared. That's 2.10 times 10 to the second kilopascals. For part b, divide 405 newtons by 12.9 square centimeters: 3.14 times 10 to the second kilopascals.

Step three: evaluate. Pressure should be in pascals, and a newton per square meter is a pascal. With fewer legs touching, the same force acts on less area, so the pressure goes up. It checks out!

testIt.name: Child on a stool
testIt.how: Tip the stool: three legs (19.3 cm²) or two legs (12.9 cm²) carrying 405 N.

7.title: Boyle's Law and Charles's Law
7.text:
Boyle's Law and Charles's Law

Boyle's law: at constant temperature, P sub 1 V sub 1 equals P sub 2 V sub 2. Charles's law: at constant pressure, V sub 1 over T sub 1 equals V sub 2 over T sub 2.

Hold a gas at constant temperature and squeeze it into a smaller volume. More particles hit the walls, so the pressure goes up. Expand it, and the pressure goes down. Seventeenth-century chemist and physicist Robert Boyle found this inverse relationship. Boyle's law says P times V is constant, or P sub 1 V sub 1 equals P sub 2 V sub 2. The subscripts track values before and after a change. Scuba divers like the one in Figure 3 depend on this! A regulator lowers the high-pressure gas from the tank to match the water pressure, so the diver can breathe.

About 100 years later, Jacques Charles cooled gases and found the volume shrank in a straight-line pattern, by one two-hundred-seventy-third of its volume at 0 degrees Celsius for each degree cooled. He couldn't reach really low temperatures, so he extended his graph. It suggested a gas would have zero volume at negative 273 degrees Celsius. That temperature is now called absolute zero, the zero of the Kelvin scale.

Charles's law says that at constant pressure, volume varies directly with Kelvin temperature: V over T is constant, or V sub 1 over T sub 1 equals V sub 2 over T sub 2.

8.title: The Combined Gas Law
8.text:
The Combined Gas Law

For a fixed amount of an ideal gas, P sub 1 V sub 1 over T sub 1 equals P sub 2 V sub 2 over T sub 2.

Put Boyle's law and Charles's law together and you get the combined gas law. For a fixed amount of ideal gas, pressure times volume divided by Kelvin temperature is constant: P sub 1 V sub 1 over T sub 1 equals P sub 2 V sub 2 over T sub 2.

Figure 4 shows how it shrinks back down. Hold temperature constant, and you get Boyle's law. Hold pressure constant, and you get Charles's law. And if you hold volume constant? Then P sub 1 over T sub 1 equals P sub 2 over T sub 2, so pressure varies directly with Kelvin temperature. That's called Gay-Lussac's law.

testIt.name: Combined law
testIt.how: Use the button to double the temperature of 2.0 L at 100 kPa and 300 K while also doubling the pressure.

9.title: The Ideal Gas Law
9.text:
The Ideal Gas Law

The ideal gas law states that pressure times volume equals the number of moles times R times the Kelvin temperature: P V equals n R T.

What does the constant in the combined gas law depend on? Keep volume and temperature fixed and add more particles, N. More collisions means more pressure. So the constant is proportional to N: P V over T equals k N, where k is Boltzmann's constant, 1.38 times 10 to the negative twenty-third pascal cubic meters per kelvin.

N is always huge, so scientists use the mole instead. A mole is like a dozen, but instead of 12 items it's 6.022 times 10 to the twenty-third particles, Avogadro's number, named for Italian scientist Amedeo Avogadro. A sample whose mass equals the substance's molar mass contains one mole, so you can convert between mass and n, the number of moles.

Using moles changes the constant to R, which is 8.31 pascal cubic meters per mole kelvin. That gives the ideal gas law: P V equals n R T. With this R, use cubic meters, kelvins, and pascals. It predicts real gases remarkably well, except at high pressures or low temperatures.

10.title: Example Problem 2, Chilling Argon
10.text:
Example Problem 2, Chilling Argon

Use the combined gas law for changing conditions and the ideal gas law to count moles.

A 20.0-liter sample of argon at 273 kelvins is at atmospheric pressure, 101.3 kilopascals. It's cooled to 120 kelvins and squeezed to 145 kilopascals. Find the new volume, the number of moles, and the mass. Argon's molar mass is 39.9 grams per mole.

Step one: analyze and sketch. Sketch the container before and after. Known: V sub 1 is 20.0 liters, P sub 1 is 101.3 kilopascals, T sub 1 is 273 kelvins, P sub 2 is 145 kilopascals, T sub 2 is 120 kelvins, R is 8.31 pascal cubic meters per mole kelvin, and M is 39.9 grams per mole. Unknown: V sub 2, the moles, and the mass.

Step two: solve. From the combined gas law, V sub 2 equals P sub 1 V sub 1 T sub 2 over P sub 2 T sub 1: 101.3 kilopascals times 20.0 liters times 120 kelvins, divided by 145 kilopascals times 273 kelvins, which is 6.1 liters. Next, n equals P V over R T: 101.3 times 10 to the third pascals times 0.0200 cubic meters, divided by 8.31 times 273 kelvins, which is 0.893 moles. Finally, m equals M n: 39.9 grams per mole times 0.893 moles, which is 35.6 grams.

Step three: evaluate. Volume is in liters and mass is in grams. The volume shrank, which fits a higher pressure and a lower temperature, and the mass is reasonable. It checks out!

testIt.name: Chilling argon
testIt.how: Change the final temperature and pressure of 20.0 L of argon at 273 K and 101.3 kPa.

11.title: Thermal Expansion and Convection
11.text:
Thermal Expansion and Convection

Thermal expansion is a property of all forms of matter that causes the matter to expand, becoming less dense, when heated.

Gases expand as they warm, and in fact all forms of matter do. That's thermal expansion: matter expands and becomes less dense when heated. It's useful, too, like for moving air around a room.

In Figure 5, air near the radiator warms, becomes less dense, and rises. Gravity pulls the denser, cooler air near the ceiling down. That air gets warmed at the radiator, and the loop keeps going. This circulation is a convection current. You'll find one in a pot of hot but not boiling water on the stove. The cooler, denser water sinks to the bottom, warms, and is pushed up by more cool water sinking from the top.

There's no perfect model for liquids, but it helps to picture one as a finely ground solid. Small groups of particles move together like tiny pieces of solid. When heated, the groups spread apart, and the whole liquid expands. For the same temperature change, liquids expand much more than solids but less than gases.

12.title: Why Ice Floats
12.text:
Why Ice Floats

Water is most dense at 4 degrees Celsius, so ice floats.

Since matter expands when heated, you might expect ice to be denser than water and sink. But water is strange! The forces between water molecules are strong, and they lock ice into crystals with a very open structure. Even after ice melts, tiny bits of that open structure remain. As water warms from 0 degrees Celsius to 4 degrees Celsius, those bits collapse and the water actually contracts.

Above 4 degrees Celsius, faster molecular motion wins, and water expands like normal. So water is densest at 4 degrees Celsius, and ice floats. That's a big deal for life on Earth! If ice sank, lakes would freeze from the bottom up each winter, and many would never fully melt in summer.

13.title: Plasma
13.text:
Plasma

Plasma is a gaslike state of negatively charged electrons and positively charged ions.

Heat a solid, and it melts. Heat it more, and it becomes a gas. Keep going? Collisions get so violent that they knock electrons off atoms, leaving positively charged ions. This gaslike mix of electrons and ions is plasma, another state of matter.

Plasma might sound rare, but it's the most common state of ordinary, visible matter in the universe! Stars are mostly plasma at extremely high temperatures, and much of the hydrogen between stars and galaxies has lost its electrons, so it's plasma too.

The main difference: plasmas conduct electric current well, while ordinary gases barely do. Lightning bolts are plasma. So are neon signs like Figure 6, and the fluorescent bulbs that may light your school. The glow's color depends on the gas in the tube.

So, what is a fluid? It's any material that flows and takes the shape of its container, like liquids, gases, and plasmas. Fluids exert pressure, follow the gas laws, expand when heated, and move in convection currents.
